query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases? Earlier studies of refractory and transition-metal-based high-entropy alloys primarily examined elemental and compositional effects involving Al, Cr, Si, Ti, and V, but the reported outcomes depended on composition limits, phase readjustment, and processing. This emphasis has not resolved the oxidation behavior of compositionally complex alloys, for which synergistic elemental effects make interpretation difficult. The starting alloy was designed to retain an fcc matrix for formability and has demonstrated notable strength and fatigue performance, so any explanation should account for its integrity without compromising those constraints. Define a controlled comparison that would distinguish the proposed explanation, predict observations relative to the starting-state baseline, identify applicable exposure boundaries and supporting prior evidence, and state an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: At high temperatures, the degradation of the additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA is governed by the selective oxidation of Cr (with minor input from Al and Ti) that produces a dual-layer oxide scale. The inner portion is enriched in Cr that forms a slow-growing, adherent barrier, whereas the outer region is less coherent. This oxide scale limits oxygen ingress via grain‐boundary diffusion, thereby preserving the fcc matrix and its excellent strength and fatigue performance. Under reducing conditions the oxide scale becomes discontinuous, leading to accelerated degradation.
generation.material_initial_state: Additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with a homogeneous single-phase fcc matrix
generation.intervention: Controlled exposure to elevated temperatures in oxidizing versus reducing gas atmospheres
generation.conditions: Temperature range of approximately 600–900 °C with exposures up to 120 hours in synthetic air (oxidizing conditions) and in a controlled reducing gas (e.g., hydrogen-containing or CO-rich atmosphere)
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a layered oxide scale featuring a continuous, Cr-rich inner layer and a more porous outer oxide layer
generation.mechanism: Selective oxidation of Cr (and minor contributions from Al and Ti) at elevated temperatures forms a coherent, protective oxide barrier that retards further oxygen diffusion via grain-boundary pathways. In oxidizing environments this barrier minimizes degradation of the underlying fcc matrix, while in reducing conditions the incomplete or discontinuous oxide scale permits faster degradation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under oxidizing conditions, a thin, continuous Cr-rich oxide layer will form, leading to slower degradation kinetics and minimal losses in macro-scale mechanical properties. In contrast, under reducing conditions, the oxide scale will be less adherent and more discontinuous, resulting in a higher rate of degradation despite retention of the fcc structure.
generation.baseline: The as-fabricated alloy with its homogeneous fcc microstructure and minimal pre-existing oxide scale
generation.boundary: The observed protective behavior should be most significant within the tested temperature window (600–900 °C) and exposure times (50–120 hours); behavior outside these regimes may not clearly demonstrate the selective oxidation effects.
generation.uncertainty: The precise role of minor alloying elements (Al and Ti) within the protective scale and the relative importance of grain-boundary versus bulk diffusion in scale formation are not fully quantified, and further detailed characterization is needed to refine these aspects.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare multiple identical samples of the alloy and subject them to identical high-temperature exposures in controlled oxidizing (synthetic air) and reducing (e.g., H2/CO mixture) atmospheres. Post-exposure, use high-resolution microscopy (SEM/TEM) and surface analysis (XPS or EDS) to characterize the oxide scale morphology, composition, and continuity. Concurrently, measure changes in mechanical properties (e.g., fatigue resistance, strength) relative to the as-fabricated baseline.
measurements: Oxide scale thickness, continuity, and chemical composition (especially Cr enrichment)
Profiles of oxygen and alloy element distribution across the scale
Residual mechanical performance (tensile strength, fatigue life)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If both oxidizing and reducing conditions produce similar oxide morphologies (e.g., no distinct Cr-rich inner layer) and exhibit comparable rates of degradation in mechanical properties, then the hypothesized role of selective Cr oxidation in governing degradation is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: As seen from Figure 4b, the higher oxide content in the coating deposited from a higher distance does not result in a higher microhardness. On the contrary, with an increase in the spaying distance from 150 mm to 250 mm, the microhardness decreases from 750 HV to 550 HV. Taking into account earlier observations, a noticeable decrease in the microhardness with an increase in the spraying distance can be explained by the increased porosity, the increase in the amount of the soft FCC phase, and the softening of the BCC solid solution due to Al outflow []. Thus, particle oxidation during high-temperature spraying in an oxygen-containing atmosphere considerably influences the coating properties.

This study uncovers the oxidation process in compositionally complex alloys. Our study involved subjecting an equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn alloy to oxidation at 400 °C under 10 mbar oxygen pressure for both ex situ and in situ observations. Ex situ observations, conducted using TEM after 120 min of oxidation, revealed a layered oxide structure. The 20 nm oxide layer on the equiatomic base alloy exhibited a composition sequence of Ni-rich (bottom layer), Cr-rich, and then Fe, Mn, and Co-rich layers (outer oxide). We chose a relatively low oxidation temperature to prevent phase transformation in the alloy, focusing solely on examining the oxidation process in the super-saturated alloy condition. High-entropy alloys (HEAs) are typically produced using high-temperature metallurgical routes; however, alternative synthesis approaches based on wet-chemical processing remain relatively unexplored. In this study, a compositionally complex two-phase AgCuCoNiFe high-entropy alloy was synthesized using a precipitation–reduction strategy involving co-precipitation of mixed metal carbonates followed by thermal reduction in a reducing atmosphere. The objective of the work was to evaluate the feasibility of this hydrometallurgical route for preparing compositionally complex alloys and to investigate the structural evolution of the material as a function of reduction time. Quantitative MP-AES analysis confirmed efficient co-precipitation of all five elements, enabling the preparation of a precursor with near-equimolar metal composition. Structural characterization using SEM, EDS, and XRD revealed the presence of surface compositional heterogeneity in the as-reduced state, characterized by Ag-enriched domains.
